primary_claim_cluster: Evaluation boundaries for scientist-agent autonomy claims
subordinate_leaf: Compare end-to-end scientist-agent demonstrations with granular scientific-task benchmarks and human-in-the-loop experimental validation.
scope_note: Clean, bounded literature slice; no old research artifacts or private worker claims were used.

sources.title: ScienceAgentBench: Toward Rigorous Assessment of Language Agents for Data-Driven Scientific Discovery
sources.finding: The benchmark contains 102 tasks derived from 44 peer-reviewed publications across four disciplines and explicitly argues for evaluating individual scientific-workflow tasks before making end-to-end automation claims. Reported best success is 32.4% without expert knowledge and 34.3% with expert-provided knowledge under three attempts; higher inference-time compute improves results but does not establish end-to-end automation.

sources.title: MLAgentBench: Evaluating Language Agents on Machine Learning Experimentation
sources.finding: Across 13 machine-learning experimentation tasks, the paper reports 37.5% average success for its best tested Claude v3 Opus agent, with success ranging from 100% on some established tasks to 0% on recent Kaggle challenges; long-term planning and hallucination are identified as key challenges.

sources.title: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
sources.finding: The work demonstrates a pipeline that generates ideas, writes code, executes experiments, visualizes results, writes papers, and runs a simulated review, applied to three machine-learning subfields. This is an end-to-end framework demonstration in a bounded computational domain; its automated-review acceptance result should not be treated as evidence of general scientific autonomy or independent external validation.

sources.title: The Virtual Lab of AI agents designs new SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies
sources.finding: The system is explicitly an AI-human collaboration: an LLM PI coordinates scientist agents while a human provides high-level feedback. It designed 92 nanobodies computationally, and human-run experimental validation identified functional candidates. The result is strong evidence for collaborative scientific utility with wet-lab validation, not evidence of fully autonomous wet-lab execution.

sources.title: Automating the practice of science: Opportunities, challenges, and implications
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(5), e2401238121 (2025)
sources.finding: This peer-reviewed perspective surveys opportunities, bottlenecks, and ethical/practical implications of scientific automation and supports treating automation as stage-specific rather than collapsing heterogeneous scientific activities into a single autonomy label.

synthesis: Current public literature supports a distinction between a demonstrated automated research pipeline and validated autonomous scientific capability. End-to-end computational demonstrations can cover many workflow stages while granular benchmarks still show substantial failure rates on executable scientific tasks.
Real-world experimental success can coexist with material human participation: the Virtual Lab couples agentic design with human high-level feedback and human wet-lab validation.

Therefore, claims about scientist agents should preserve distinctions among mechanism, framework demonstration, benchmarked task capability, human-AI collaboration, empirical validation, and deployed autonomous operation.
hypothesis_from_literature: A robust evaluation rubric for scientist agents should report at least five separable dimensions: (1) ideation/planning quality, (2) executable analysis or experiment construction, (3) empirical/physical validation, (4) degree and location of human intervention, and (5) independence of evaluation/review. This rubric is an inference from the cited literature, not a directly validated benchmark result in this slice.
limitations: This slice does not compare every available scientist-agent benchmark or system.
The AI Scientist result is a computational-machine-learning framework demonstration and uses simulated review; it is not evidence of independent production deployment.
The Virtual Lab provides experimentally validated outputs but explicitly includes human feedback and human experimental execution.
Benchmark percentages are study-specific and should not be compared as if they shared identical task distributions or evaluation protocols.
